senses.gloss:
snātaka
(‘one who has taken the [ceremonial] bath [after studenthood]’)
------------------------------------------
A ब्रह्मचारिन् (a Vedic student living in the होउसे of his गुरु) was expected to take a ceremonial bath at the end of his student-period and seek the permission of his गुरु to return home, after paying the गुरुदक्षिणा (fees). Such an one was called ‘snātaka’.
Snātakas were of three types: vidyāsnātaka (one who had finished the course of Vedic studies but had not kept the वेदव्रतस् or Vedic vows); vrata-स्नातक (one who had kept the vows but could not complete the course in the stipulated period); vidyāvratasnātaka (one who had finished both).
The last one was considered the best of the three and was highly respected.
He could then return home and settle down as a गृहस्थ or householder.
A स्नातक could be introduced to an assemblage of learned men by his गुरु.
The धर्मशास्त्रस् give innumerable rules for a स्नातक to observe. Most of them are concerned with his physical safety and maintenance of the purity of his life.
See also SAMĀVARTANA.

Snānayātrā
------------------------------------------
The pūrṇimā during the month of Jyeṣṭha—Jyeṣṭhapūrṇimā (May-June)—is known as the स्नानयात्रा day. This is the day on which Lord Jagannātha (of पुरी) is said to have incarnated himself in the present form of that image. On this occasion all the three images are brought out of the temple on to a platform and anointed by 108 pitchers of sacred water to the accompaniment of मुसिच् and Vedic chants. The images are then dressed in resplendent clothes.
See also JAGANNĀTHA PURĪ and RATHAYĀTRĀ.

snāna
(‘bath’)
------------------------------------------
In the life of a Hindu, even ordinary acts like स्नान or bathing, needed to keep the body clean and pure, are considered a sacrament that elevates one spiritually.
A bath is compulsory for persons of all varṇas. It is to be taken in a river, a big tank, the tank attached to a temple, or from the water drawn from one’s own well or even a public well.
The ब्राह्मण householders are expected to take bath twice—before sunrise and at noon—whereas a ब्रह्मचारिन् is to take it only once. A saṁnyāsin should bathe thrice, the last one being before sunset.
The bath should always be accompanied by the chanting of Vedic mantras such as Ṛgveda (10.9.1-3), Taittirīya Saṁhitā (5.6.1.1, 2) and Ṛgveda (10.190.1-3).
When a person is unable to take bath as prescribed (with all the formalities and mantras) shortcuts are permitted such as invoking river-goddesses into the water and sprinkling the same over himself.
Some of the पुराणस् and smṛtis (vide Śaṅkhasmṛti 8.1 to 11; Agnipurāna 155.3, 4) give a list of six varieties of स्नान. They are: नित्य, naimittika, kāmya, kriyāṅga, malāpakarṣaṇa (or अभ्यङ्ग) and kriyā.
Nityasnāna is the one already described.
Naimittikasnāna is occasioned by a निमित्त or a special reason like the birth of a son or the completion of a sacrifice or an एच्लिप्से and so on.
Kāmyasnāna (bath for some desired object) is undertaken in a place of पिल्ग्रिमगे or at any other place.
Kriyāṅgasnāna is resorted to as a part of a religious rite.
Malāpakarṣaṇa स्नान is actually an oilbath undertaken on certain auspicious days to get prosperity.
Kriyāsnāna is the bathing done at a place of पिल्ग्रिमगे to get the merit and performed as per the procedure prescribed (vide Śaṅkhasmṛti 9).
The धर्मशास्त्रस् have also enume-rated six kinds of gauṇasnāna (secondary baths). They are: मन्त्रस्नान (sprinkling water over oneself with certain mantras); bhaumasnāna (smearing the body with loose earth); āgneyasnāna (applying holy ashes); vāyavīyasnāna (taking on or exposing the body to the dust raised by the hoofs of cows); divyasnāna (wetting one’s body in a shower of rain accompanied by sunshine) and mānasasnāna (repeating the name of God in the मिन्द्).
